title: The Comedy of Errors
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Ephesus, a trading city on the Aegean, from late morning until five in the afternoon
lengthNote: About 1,777 lines — the shortest play in the Folio
openingLine: Proceed, Solinus, to procure my fall
summary: Two sets of identical twins, separated by shipwreck when they were babies, spend one day in the same city without meeting. Antipholus of Syracuse has come looking for the brother he cannot remember; Antipholus of Ephesus is already settled there, with a wife, a house and a goldsmith's account, and loses all three by teatime. Every disaster follows the same mechanism: a servant is sent on an errand, does it correctly, and reports to the wrong master. Around that Roman machine Shakespeare builds a frame of his own invention — a father under sentence of death at sunset, and the wife he lost at sea waiting inside the abbey he walks past all day.

sourceText.label: Project Gutenberg text of the Complete Works of William Shakespeare (eBook 100)
sourceText.note: The quotations are taken word for word from this text, and act, scene and line references follow the traditional Globe numbering, which modern editions vary from by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Verse tests place it among the first plays; the Gray's Inn performance of December 1594 is the latest it can have been finished.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto exists. The First Folio prints it among the Comedies under the title The Comedie of Errors.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: The Menaechmi gives the twins, Amphitruo the husband shut out of his own house; the second pair of twins, Egeon, Emilia and the abbey are Shakespeare's.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: One city, one afternoon, and about 1,777 lines: the shortest play Shakespeare wrote.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Egeon’s story, and the first mistake
structure.summary: The play opens with an execution scheduled for sunset. Egeon of Syracuse has landed in Ephesus against the trade law, and buys an hour of the Duke's attention by explaining how he came to be looking for his family: a wife, two sons and two bought servants, torn apart when the ship struck a rock and each half of the mast was picked up by a different vessel. He is given one day to raise a thousand marks. The second scene puts his surviving son ashore in the same city, where a servant he does not own hands him the first mistake.

scenes.title: The Duke's hall
scenes.summary: Egeon is condemned under a law about Syracusan merchants, tells the story of the wreck that scattered his household, and is given until evening to find the ransom.

scenes.title: The mart
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Syracuse sends his Dromio to the inn with a thousand marks, then meets the other Dromio, who wants him home to a dinner he knows nothing about, and is beaten for it.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A wife claims the wrong husband
structure.summary: Adriana waits for a man who does not come, and argues with her unmarried sister about whether a wife owes more obedience than a husband owes attendance. Her servant comes back beaten for the second time that day. Then she finds the wrong Antipholus in the street, delivers the most serious speech in the play to a complete stranger, and takes him home to dinner with the door bolted behind them.

scenes.title: Dinner going cold
scenes.summary: Adriana and Luciana quarrel in couplets about liberty in marriage; Dromio of Ephesus reports that his master denies house, wife and gold.

scenes.title: The wrong husband taken home
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Syracuse beats his own Dromio for a conversation he never had, then is claimed as a husband by a woman he has never seen, and decides to play along.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: The locked door
structure.summary: The husband who belongs in the house arrives at his own door with a merchant, a goldsmith and an appetite, and is shouted down through it by his brother's servant while his wife tells him to go away. Talked out of breaking in with a crowbar, he walks off to dine with a courtesan and promises her the gold chain his wife was to have had. Meanwhile his brother is courting his wife's sister.

scenes.title: Shut out of his own house
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Ephesus is shouted down through his own front door by his brother's Dromio, Luce the kitchen maid and Adriana, argued out of forcing it, and goes off to dine at the Porpentine and give the chain away out of spite.

scenes.title: Courtship and the kitchen wench
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Syracuse makes love to Luciana in rhyme; Dromio flees Nell's claim on him; Angelo hands over the chain to a man who never ordered it.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Debt, arrest and a conjurer
structure.summary: Money makes a domestic muddle into a legal one. Angelo is pressed by his own creditor, presses Antipholus of Ephesus for a chain the man never received, and has him arrested in the street. The bail is fetched by the wrong servant and handed to the wrong master. The courtesan reports her ring stolen. By the end of the act a hedge-priest called Pinch has declared master and man possessed, and both are tied up in a dark cellar.

scenes.title: The arrest
scenes.summary: Angelo, squeezed for a debt he cannot pay, has Antipholus of Ephesus taken by an officer over a chain that is at that moment round his brother's neck.

scenes.title: The purse of ducats
scenes.summary: Dromio of Syracuse brings Adriana the news of an arrest and carries her bail money away to a prisoner who is not his master.

scenes.title: Strangers with gifts
scenes.summary: Greeted by name, offered goods and handed gold all over town, Antipholus of Syracuse decides that Ephesus is full of witches and will not give the Courtesan her ring.

scenes.title: Doctor Pinch
scenes.summary: Antipholus of Ephesus beats his Dromio for bringing a rope instead of bail, is examined by a conjurer, and is bound and carried home as a madman.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Both pairs on stage together
structure.summary: Everyone arrives in the same square. The Syracusans take sanctuary in the priory; the Ephesians gnaw through their bonds and come to the Duke for justice; Egeon, walking to the block, recognises a son who does not recognise him. Then the Abbess brings the second pair out through the gate, the two Antipholuses stand side by side, and she turns out to be Egeon's wife. Four acts of taking a family apart are undone in the last hundred lines.

scenes.title: Before the priory
scenes.summary: Sanctuary, an execution procession, two flatly contradictory sworn accounts of the same day, and the moment both pairs finally stand in the same square.

characters.name: Antipholus of Syracuse
characters.role: A traveller searching for his lost twin and mother
characters.summary: He left Syracuse at eighteen and has spent seven years looking for a brother he would not know by sight, and says so in the play's most famous image: a drop of water gone into the sea to find another drop. Ephesus answers him with gold, dinner invitations and a wife, none of which he asked for, and he decides in 2.2 to take what is offered and see where it leads.
characters.clue: He says he is but two hours old in Ephesus, and compares himself to a drop of water searching the sea for another drop.

characters.name: Antipholus of Ephesus
characters.role: A merchant of Ephesus, married to Adriana
characters.summary: He is the twin with everything to lose: a standing in the city, a wife, a goldsmith who trusts him and a soldier's claim on the Duke's gratitude. In a single afternoon he is shut out of his house, refused his dinner, arrested for a chain he never touched, declared insane by a quack and tied up in his own cellar. He never once doubts who he is, which is why he is the angriest man on stage.
characters.clue: He is kept out of his own front door at dinner time, and sends a servant for a crowbar.

characters.name: Dromio of Syracuse
characters.summary: He is the quicker of the two Dromios and does most of the joking, making a beating into an argument about Father Time’s bald head and a fat kitchen maid into a map of Europe. He is also the only character who guesses correctly what is happening to them, deciding early that Ephesus is fairy land and that everyone in it means to pinch them black and blue.
characters.clue: He plays porter at a door he has no right to, and escapes a marriage to a woman he describes as spherical.

relationships.label: twin brother of, and mistaken for
takes orders from, as her husband's man

characters.name: Dromio of Ephesus
characters.summary: He is beaten by two masters and a mistress in a single day for carrying messages accurately. His complaints are the play's running account of what service costs: sent between house and mart like a football, marked on the head instead of paid in marks, and beaten at last for buying the rope's end his master told him to buy. He gets the last speech of the play, and uses it to take his brother's hand.
characters.clue: He is sent out to buy a rope's end, brings it back, and is beaten because his master had meant to send him for bail.

relationships.label: twin brother of, and mistaken for

characters.name: Adriana
characters.summary: She is jealous, and she is right: her husband spends the afternoon at a courtesan's table and promises his wife's gold chain to the woman sitting across it. Shakespeare gives her the longest and best speech in the play, an argument that a marriage cannot be divided any more than one drop of water can be taken back out of the sea, and then has her deliver it to a man she has never met.
characters.clue: She makes the play's finest speech about marriage to a stranger, and locks the front door on her own husband.

relationships.label: lectured on jealousy by, and refused entry
married at his urging, and appeals to him for justice

characters.name: Luciana
characters.summary: She preaches wifely obedience with the confidence of someone who has never been married, telling her sister that beasts, fishes and fowls are all subject to their males. Courted by the wrong Antipholus, she gives him advice she cannot have meant to give: if you must be unfaithful, do it quietly and be kind at the table. Her own feelings are never stated: in the last scene the right Antipholus promises to make good what his brother said to her, and she says nothing at all.
characters.clue: She argues for obedience before marriage, and advises a man she thinks is her brother-in-law to lie better.

characters.name: Egeon
characters.role: A merchant of Syracuse, condemned to die at sunset
characters.summary: He opens the play asking to be executed and spends a hundred lines telling the Duke why, in a speech of shipwreck and a mast cut in half that belongs to romance and not to farce. He then disappears for three acts. When he comes back, on his way to the block, his own son looks at him and says he has never seen him before. The Folio prints his name as Egeon; modern editions often set it as Aegeon.
characters.clue: He tells the story of the split mast, then vanishes until the headsman brings him back in the last scene.

relationships.label: husband of, parted at sea from

characters.name: Emilia
characters.role: Abbess of the priory at Ephesus, and Egeon's wife
characters.summary: She appears for the first time in the last scene, refuses to hand over the man who has taken sanctuary with her, and takes Adriana apart on the subject of nagging with a thoroughness nobody else in the play manages. Then she recognises her husband. In her closing speech the whole day becomes a birth she has been waiting thirty-three years to finish.
characters.clue: She has lived in the abbey the whole time, and does not appear until the last scene, when she claims both twins and a husband.

relationships.label: wife of, lost at sea from
mother of, and giver of sanctuary to

characters.name: Solinus
characters.summary: He enforces a law he plainly dislikes, tells Egeon that his own crown and oath stop him from doing what he would prefer, and then gives him the day anyway. In the last scene he is handed two sworn accounts of the same afternoon that cannot both be true, and reaches for the only explanation available: they have all been drinking from Circe's cup.
characters.clue: He sentences a man in the first scene and spends the last one trying to work out which of two identical men is the real one.

relationships.label: urged her marriage by letter, and hears her suit

characters.name: Angelo
characters.summary: He makes the chain that ruins everybody. Owing money to a merchant who is about to sail, he needs payment for a necklace he handed to the wrong Antipholus in the street, and has the right one arrested when he denies taking it. He is neither a villain nor a fool: he is a tradesman with a debt due, and his credit is the only thing he has.
characters.clue: He delivers a gold chain unasked to a stranger in the street, then has a different man arrested for not paying for it.

relationships.label: goldsmith to, and giver of the wrong chain

themes.name: Identity
themes.summary: The play removes one proof at a time. A name fails, because two men answer to it. A face fails, because two men have it. Servants, wives, creditors and sworn witnesses all fail. Only the sight of both twins standing together settles anything, which makes the ending a visual event and not an argument.
themes.development: Antipholus of Syracuse loses himself on purpose in 1.2; by 2.2 he wonders whether he is in earth, heaven or hell; in 5.1 the Duke has to ask outright which of two men is the natural one.

themes.name: Marriage, obedience and jealousy
themes.summary: Adriana and Luciana open the second act with a formal argument about whether a wife’s liberty should match her husband’s, and the play puts both positions to the proof. Adriana's jealousy turns out to be justified, and she is still the one blamed for the household's collapse by the woman who turns out to be her mother-in-law.
themes.development: The couplet debate of 2.1 sets the terms; Adriana's speech in 2.2 raises the stakes; Luciana coaches adultery in 3.2; and the Abbess delivers the verdict against Adriana in 5.1.

themes.name: Service and the beaten servant
themes.summary: Both Dromios were bought as infants to attend the twins, and both spend the day being struck for errands they carried out correctly. The beatings are staged as farce and described by the victims as a working life, which is where the play's comedy sits closest to something else.
themes.development: The first blow falls in 1.2 and Dromio of Ephesus is threatened with another in 2.1; by 4.4 he can list what service has paid him, sorted by weather, from cold mornings to a lame beggar's old age.

themes.name: Debt, bonds and the price of a life
themes.summary: Ephesus runs on credit. A man's life costs a thousand marks, a chain costs two hundred ducats, and a goldsmith who cannot collect must have a customer arrested to keep his own name good. Every crisis in the middle acts is triggered by somebody needing to be paid on time.
themes.development: The ransom is set in 1.1; the chain is ordered in 3.1 and misdelivered in 3.2; the arrest in 4.1 follows a creditor's own deadline, and the ducats sent as bail go astray in 4.2.

themes.name: Time
themes.summary: Characters announce the hour constantly: two o'clock, five o'clock, dinner time, the dial pointing at five, sunset for the execution. The whole plot runs on people being late, and the servants build their best jokes out of Father Time's bald head and time as a bankrupt who owes more than he is worth.
themes.development: Dinner is already spoiling in 1.2, Adriana counts the hours in 2.1, Dromio runs a comic case on Time in 2.2 and 4.2, and the Merchant's sighting of the dial at five in 5.1 brings the execution party on.

themes.name: Being shut out
themes.summary: Dinner is the thing everybody is trying to get to and almost nobody eats. A house with a locked door and the wrong family inside it is the play’s central image, and it is staged so that the audience sees both sides of the same door.
themes.development: The dinner is announced in 1.2, taken by the wrong guest in 2.2, denied to the right one in 3.1, and replaced at the end by an invitation into the abbey for a gossips' feast.

themes.name: Witchcraft, possession and being called mad
themes.summary: Ephesus was known for sorcery long before this play, and the Syracusans reach for that explanation within an hour of landing. The Ephesians reach for the same one about them. Being declared mad has hard consequences here: a conjurer is hired, a man is tied up, and only sanctuary stops the treatment going further.
themes.development: Antipholus of Syracuse names the town's jugglers and witches in 1.2; by 4.3 he thinks the Courtesan is the devil; in 4.4 Pinch has the other twin bound, and the Abbess proposes syrups and prayers in 5.1.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Building a plot out of two figures who cannot be told apart, so that every entrance can be a mistake.
techniques.inThisBook: Plautus used one pair of twins. Shakespeare uses two, which means errors can cross between master and servant as well as between brother and brother, and it means the last scene needs four actors on stage who look like two.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: Letting the audience hold a piece of information every character on stage lacks.
techniques.inThisBook: The audience is told in the first scene that two sets of twins exist, and then watches everyone else work without that fact for four acts. The jokes are in the gap between the lines, which is why the play reads thin and plays fast.

techniques.name: Line-for-line exchange
techniques.definition: Dialogue in which speakers alternate single lines, often rhyming, so that the argument becomes a contest of form.
techniques.inThisBook: Adriana and Luciana open 2.1 trading rhymed couplets on liberty in marriage, and the Abbess breaks Adriana down in 5.1 by cutting her answers shorter and shorter until she runs out of them.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.definition: Puns and quibbles pressed until the word gives way.
techniques.inThisBook: Marks on a pate against marks in gold, a sconce that is a head and a fort, a rope’s end that is also an end in view, and a bond that is a debt and a set of cords gnawed through with the teeth.

techniques.name: Catalogue
techniques.definition: A list allowed to run well past its point, until the accumulation becomes the joke.
techniques.inThisBook: Dromio of Syracuse maps a kitchen maid onto Europe country by country in 3.2, and lists everything a sergeant is in 4.3. Dromio of Ephesus answers a question about his working life in 4.4 with a catalogue of beatings sorted by weather.

techniques.name: The set piece
techniques.definition: A self-contained episode built to a single effect, playable almost as its own short scene.
techniques.inThisBook: The lock-out at 3.1 is the clearest example: two servants shouting through a door in rhyming fourteeners while a husband, a goldsmith and a dinner guest stand in the street. It works on stage whatever a production does with the rest of the play.

techniques.name: The classical unities
techniques.definition: Keeping a play to one place, one day and one line of action.
techniques.inThisBook: One city, one afternoon, one mistake repeated. This and The Tempest are the only plays Shakespeare wrote to that Roman rule, and here it supplies the pressure: nobody has time to compare notes, so each error survives long enough to cause the next.

quotations.text: Again, if any Syracusian born Come to the bay of Ephesus, he dies, His goods confiscate to the Duke's dispose, Unless a thousand marks be levied To quit the penalty and to ransom him.
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: The Duke explaining to Egeon why he cannot be spared.
quotations.analysis: A comedy opens with a trade embargo read out in full. The law is reciprocal, not cruel by design (Syracuse does the same to Ephesians), and the sum is what matters: a man’s life is quoted at a price, and the rest of the play moves smaller sums of money to the wrong people.

quotations.text: A heavier task could not have been impos'd Than I to speak my griefs unspeakable
quotations.speaker: Egeon
quotations.context: Beginning the account of the shipwreck, at the Duke's request.
quotations.analysis: The line that launches a hundred lines of narrative says the story cannot be told. 'Unspeakable' is doing two jobs: too painful to say, and too large for speech. Nothing else in the play sounds like this, and the register only returns when Egeon does, in the last scene, to a son who does not know his voice.

quotations.text: I to the world am like a drop of water That in the ocean seeks another drop, Who, failing there to find his fellow forth, Unseen, inquisitive, confounds himself.
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Alone on the mart, having sent his servant to the inn.
quotations.analysis: ‘Confounds’ means defeats and also mingles, so the drop searching the sea is lost in the same motion that dissolves it. He states the play's problem before any error has happened: a man looking for his double risks becoming indistinguishable from what he is looking for. Adriana will take the same image back off him in 2.2 and use it about marriage.

quotations.text: The clock hath strucken twelve upon the bell; My mistress made it one upon my cheek.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Explaining to the wrong master why dinner is spoiling.
quotations.analysis: Two strokes, two meanings, one word. The joke makes a household bell into a slap and gets a laugh, and it also tells the audience exactly what this servant’s day is like. Shakespeare keeps the pun running: the blows are marks, the marks are money, and the money is what everyone is shouting about.

quotations.text: They say this town is full of cozenage, As nimble jugglers that deceive the eye, Dark-working sorcerers that change the mind, Soul-killing witches that deform the body
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: After his first encounter with the wrong Dromio, who has apparently stolen his gold.
quotations.analysis: Ephesus had this reputation in Acts 19, where converts burn their books of magic, and Shakespeare cashes it in early so that every later mistake has an explanation waiting. The three trades are graded — eye, mind, body — and the play then proceeds to deceive the eye, change the mind and, in Pinch's hands, get at the body.

quotations.text: A man is master of his liberty; Time is their master, and when they see time, They'll go or come.
quotations.speaker: Luciana
quotations.context: Telling her sister not to fret about a husband who has missed dinner.
quotations.analysis: The advice is given by a woman with no husband, and it concedes the argument it means to close: if time is a man's master, the wife waiting at home is mastered by him at one more remove. Adriana spots it immediately and asks the obvious question in the next line.

quotations.text: A wretched soul bruis'd with adversity, We bid be quiet when we hear it cry; But were we burd'ned with like weight of pain, As much, or more, we should ourselves complain
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Answering her sister's recommendation of patience.
quotations.analysis: It is the best reply in the scene and it is about more than marriage: patience is cheap for whoever is not carrying the weight. Adriana ends by telling Luciana that the advice will vanish the day she is wronged herself, and the play proves her right within two acts, when Luciana is the one being courted by a man she thinks is her sister's husband.

quotations.text: Am I so round with you, as you with me, That like a football you do spurn me thus? You spurn me hence, and he will spurn me hither.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Sent back to the mart by Adriana, after a beating from the master he takes for his own.
quotations.analysis: 'Round' means plain-spoken and also spherical, and the pun holds the whole complaint: he is spoken to bluntly and kicked like a ball between two houses. In his next line he asks to be cased in leather, which is what a football was made of, so the joke ends with a servant requesting armour.

quotations.text: For know, my love, as easy mayst thou fall A drop of water in the breaking gulf, And take unmingled thence that drop again Without addition or diminishing, As take from me thyself, and not me too.
quotations.speaker: Adriana
quotations.context: Addressing a man she believes is her husband, in the street.
quotations.analysis: She picks up the image her brother-in-law used about himself an hour earlier and makes it a marriage argument: two people mixed like water cannot be separated out by weight. The speech is the most serious thing in the play and it is delivered, without anyone knowing, to the wrong man, which is the cruellest joke Shakespeare plays on anybody here.

quotations.text: Am I in earth, in heaven, or in hell? Sleeping or waking, mad, or well-advis'd? Known unto these, and to myself disguis'd!
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Being led indoors to dine as another woman's husband.
quotations.analysis: 'Known unto these, and to myself disguis'd' is the exact reverse of every other disguise plot on the Elizabethan stage: he is not hiding from them, he is hidden from himself by their certainty. Three lines later he decides to go along with it, which is what keeps the play running — the one man who could stop the errors chooses the dinner.

quotations.text: If the skin were parchment, and the blows you gave were ink, Your own handwriting would tell you what I think.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Insisting to his master that he really was beaten at the mart earlier that day.
quotations.analysis: The servant offers his body as legal evidence, in a city where documents settle everything. Parchment, ink and handwriting are the instruments of the bonds and bills that drive the middle of the play, and he turns them on his master: the marks are a signed statement, and the signature is his master's.

quotations.text: For slander lives upon succession, For ever hous'd where it gets possession.
quotations.speaker: Balthasar
quotations.context: Persuading Antipholus of Ephesus not to break down his own door.
quotations.analysis: 'Hous'd' and 'possession' are chosen with care by a man standing outside a house he cannot get into. Balthasar's point is practical: force the door and the street will invent a reason. It is also the moment the play turns, because taking the advice sends Antipholus to a courtesan and puts the chain into the wrong hands.

quotations.text: Teach sin the carriage of a holy saint, Be secret-false. What need she be acquainted? What simple thief brags of his own attaint?
quotations.speaker: Luciana
quotations.context: Lecturing the man she takes for her sister's husband on how to conduct an affair.
quotations.analysis: The sister who spent the second act preaching obedience now coaches adultery, and her objection was never to the sin. ‘Attaint’ is a legal word for being convicted and corrupted, which makes her advice a plea to avoid the verdict and keep the offence.

quotations.text: O, train me not, sweet mermaid, with thy note To drown me in thy sister's flood of tears.
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: Answering Luciana's advice with a declaration of love.
quotations.analysis: He comes back to water: a drop looking for a drop in the first act, and now a mermaid whose song would drown him in another woman’s weeping. ‘Train’ means to lure. The man who came to Ephesus searching has stopped searching, and the play never says whether he has found anything or merely stopped caring.

quotations.text: She is spherical, like a globe. I could find out countries in her.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: Describing the kitchen maid who has claimed him as her husband.
quotations.analysis: What follows is a tour of Europe conducted over a woman's body — Ireland in the bogs, Spain in her hot breath, America on a nose set with rubies. It is the longest joke in the play and the least comfortable one now, and the man making it is terrified: he is describing someone who knew the moles and warts on his body without being told.

quotations.text: Time is a very bankrupt, and owes more than he's worth to season.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Syracuse
quotations.context: Explaining to Adriana why the clock has struck one after striking two.
quotations.analysis: Everything in Ephesus can be put on account, including the hours. Dromio has just come from watching his master arrested for debt, and the joke is that the afternoon itself has run out of credit and is turning back to avoid the sergeant. It is nonsense, and it is also an exact description of a day in which nothing is paid for on time.

quotations.text: The fellow is distract, and so am I, And here we wander in illusions. Some blessed power deliver us from hence!
quotations.speaker: Antipholus of Syracuse
quotations.context: After being greeted by name, offered goods and handed a purse of gold all over town.
quotations.analysis: What unnerves him is kindness. He is not being robbed: he is greeted by name, shown silk cut to his measure and handed a purse of gold. A whole city has taken him for somebody, he cannot find out who, and the prayer is the point at which he stops trying to explain it.

quotations.text: I am an ass indeed; you may prove it by my long ears. … When I am cold, he heats me with beating; when I am warm he cools me with beating.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: Beaten for bringing back the rope's end he was sent to buy, by a master who meant to send him for bail.
quotations.analysis: The speech starts as a pun and turns into an account of a whole life, from the hour of his nativity to the day he expects to beg at doors with a limp his master gave him. Both Dromios call themselves asses repeatedly, and this is the point at which the audience is invited to hear the word as a job description.

quotations.text: The venom clamours of a jealous woman Poisons more deadly than a mad dog's tooth.
quotations.speaker: Abbess
quotations.context: Having questioned Adriana about how she treated her husband.
quotations.analysis: The Abbess presses the same point four times, not rough enough, not in private only, not enough, until Adriana boasts of how hard she nagged, and then the Abbess makes the boast a diagnosis. Luciana protests; Adriana says she was betrayed to her own reproof. Nothing later withdraws the charge, and it is spoken, though nobody on stage yet knows it, by Adriana's own mother-in-law.

quotations.text: Why, what an intricate impeach is this! I think you all have drunk of Circe's cup.
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: After hearing two sworn accounts of the day that cannot both be true.
quotations.analysis: 'Impeach' is an accusation and 'intricate' means tangled, so the Duke names the problem precisely: this is a legal tangle, not a mystery. Circe turned men into swine, and his guess is that everyone has been transformed. He is wrong about the cause and right about the effect, which is roughly where the audience has been sitting for four acts.

quotations.text: O! grief hath chang'd me since you saw me last, And careful hours with time's deformed hand, Have written strange defeatures in my face.
quotations.speaker: Egeon
quotations.context: Recognising a son who says he has never seen him before.
quotations.analysis: 'Defeatures' means disfigurements, and the writing image returns from Dromio's parchment joke in a register nobody is laughing at. The old man has been condemned, reprieved for a day, and now denied by his own child, who is telling the truth. Shakespeare lets that stand for some fifty lines before the Abbess comes back through the priory gate.

quotations.text: One of these men is genius to the other; And so of these, which is the natural man, And which the spirit? Who deciphers them?
quotations.speaker: Duke
quotations.context: Seeing both pairs of twins together for the first time.
quotations.analysis: A 'genius' was a person's attendant spirit, so the Duke's first thought is that one of each pair must be a spirit and not a man. 'Deciphers' treats the two bodies as a code somebody must read. It is the question the whole play has been asking, put by the one person with the authority to settle it, and he cannot.

quotations.text: Thirty-three years have I but gone in travail Of you, my sons, and till this present hour My heavy burden ne'er delivered.
quotations.speaker: Abbess
quotations.context: Inviting the whole company into the abbey after recognising her husband and sons.
quotations.analysis: ‘Travail’ is both labour and hardship, and she takes the metaphor all the way: the day’s confusion has been a delivery, and it has taken thirty-three years. The number does not fit the rest of the play, which points to twenty-five or so, and editors have argued about it since the eighteenth century without agreeing on a fix.

quotations.text: We came into the world like brother and brother, And now let's go hand in hand, not one before another.
quotations.speaker: Dromio of Ephesus
quotations.context: The last two lines of the play, settling which twin should walk first.
quotations.analysis: Shakespeare gives the final couplet to a servant, who uses it to set aside the question the whole play has been about: which of the two is which, and which comes first. The Antipholuses have gone off to a feast with their parents. The Dromios, who own nothing and were bought as infants, decide seniority by walking in together.

timeline.label: Plautus writes the Menaechmi, about this time
timeline.detail: A Roman farce about identical twins separated as children, one of whom arrives in the city where the other lives.

timeline.label: Plautus printed at Venice
timeline.detail: Giorgio Merula's edition, the first in print, put the Latin comedies into circulation across Europe and in time into Elizabethan grammar schools.

timeline.label: Written, probably in the early 1590s
timeline.detail: Verse tests and the heavy use of rhyme group it with the earliest plays; no record survives of its first performance.

timeline.label: Played at Gray's Inn on 28 December
timeline.detail: Gesta Grayorum describes an evening of such disorder that the revels were remembered afterwards as the Night of Errors.

timeline.label: William Warner's English Menaechmi printed
timeline.detail: Entered in the Stationers' Register in June 1594. Shakespeare could read the Latin, so whether he used the translation is disputed.

timeline.label: Performed at court on 28 December
timeline.detail: A second festive-season record, ten years to the day after Gray's Inn, showing the play still in the company's repertory.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text. It prints among the Comedies as The Comedie of Errors, with no quarto behind it and few textual problems.

timeline.label: See If You Like It; or, 'Tis All a Mistake
timeline.detail: An anonymous two-act farce at Covent Garden, cut down from Plautus and Shakespeare together.

timeline.label: Thomas Hull's The Twins
timeline.detail: Hull's alteration was played at Covent Garden on 24 April 1762 and, so far as the bills show, not again; it survived in print.

timeline.label: Samuel Phelps at Sadler's Wells
timeline.detail: Phelps played the full text in place of the Georgian alterations; reviewers called it crude and extravagant, and the house laughed anyway.

timeline.label: The Boys from Syracuse opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Rodgers and Hart's musical, directed by George Abbott, became the play's most successful afterlife and dropped its title entirely.

timeline.label: Trevor Nunn's RSC musical
timeline.detail: Music by Guy Woolfenden, lyrics by Nunn himself, choreography by Gillian Lynne, Judi Dench as Adriana; it transferred to the Aldwych and won the Olivier Award for Best New Musical.

places.name: Ephesus
places.note: Where the whole play takes place: a Greek trading city on the coast of Asia Minor, famous in Shakespeare's day for magic and for St Paul's letter.

places.name: Syracuse
places.note: Egeon's home, and the city whose merchants Ephesus has barred on pain of death.

places.name: Epidamnum
places.note: Modern Durrës, the port Egeon traded with and was sailing home from when the ship broke up; also the setting of Plautus's Menaechmi.

places.name: Corinth
places.note: The fishermen of Corinth took Emilia's half of the family; Antipholus of Ephesus was brought from there to Ephesus by Duke Menaphon.

places.name: Epidaurus
places.note: The second ship sighted after the storm, named by Egeon as it bore down on the wreck.

places.name: Gray's Inn, London
places.note: Where the play was staged on 28 December 1594, on the night the Inn's own revels collapsed into chaos.

criticalViews.summary: The oldest view treats the play as an apprentice exercise in Roman comedy: a machine of entrances and mistakes, brilliantly built and emotionally empty, worth studying for its craft and its speed.
criticalViews.counter: The frame is not farce. Egeon's hundred lines on the wreck, his son's failure to know his voice, and Emilia's speech on thirty-three years of labour are written in a register Plautus never used, and a production that plays only the machine has to cut or hurry them.

criticalViews.position: Ephesus was chosen for St Paul
criticalViews.summary: Acts 19 gives Ephesus its exorcists, its sorcerers and its burnt books of magic, and Ephesians 5 gives the doctrine of wives and husbands as one flesh that Luciana preaches and Adriana argues from. On this reading the city is a theological choice, and the abbey ending completes it.
criticalViews.counter: The play quotes no scripture and names no Christian doctrine, and everything that happens in Ephesus can be accounted for by Plautus, who set his twin plot in a port full of sharpers without any help from Paul.

criticalViews.position: Adriana is the play's serious voice
criticalViews.summary: Her speech on the drop of water in the breaking gulf is the finest writing in the play, her jealousy is factually correct, and the errors she is punished for are not hers. Read this way, the comedy contains a real marriage in trouble.
criticalViews.counter: The play gives her no vindication: the Abbess blames her in the last scene, Luciana's protest is brushed aside, and Adriana herself concedes the point. A reading that makes her the moral centre has to argue against the ending.

essayQuestions.question: How does The Comedy of Errors make a single mistake last five acts?
essayQuestions.focus: Plot mechanics, doubling and the classical unities
plan: Set out the design: one city, one afternoon, two masters and two servants who look alike, and no character who possesses the information the audience is given in 1.1.
Trace the first error through 1.2 and show that nobody does anything wrong — the servant delivers his message correctly to the wrong man.
Use 3.1 to show how the errors start feeding each other: being shut out sends Antipholus of Ephesus to the Porpentine, which is why the chain goes to the wrong brother.
Show how money raises the stakes in Act IV, where a private muddle becomes an arrest, a diagnosis and a locked cellar.
Argue about the ending: whether the recognition in 5.1 resolves the design or simply stops it, and what the Duke's inability to decipher the twins adds.

essayQuestions.question: 'The Dromios pay for everybody else's mistakes.' How far do you agree?
plan: Establish the terms: both Dromios were bought as infants from a poor woman at the inn, as Egeon explains in 1.1.
Count the beatings and say who gives them — two masters and a mistress, all for errands carried out correctly.
Look closely at the language: marks on a pate against marks in gold in 1.2, parchment and handwriting in 3.1, the catalogue of beatings by weather in 4.4.
Weigh the comedy against the complaint, and decide whether the jokes protect the audience from the violence or make it visible.
Finish with the last two lines of the play, which give the servants the closing couplet and the only settlement anybody reaches by agreement.

essayQuestions.question: What does the play make of marriage?
plan: Start with the couplet debate at the opening of 2.1 and state each sister's position exactly.
Read Adriana's speech at 2.2.112 as an argument, not a complaint, and note who she is actually speaking to.
Turn to Luciana at 3.2, where the defender of obedience recommends concealment, and ask what has changed.
Set the Abbess's verdict at 5.1.71 against everything the audience knows about the husband's afternoon at the Porpentine.
Decide what the reunion settles: the play ends with a feast and a restored family, and says nothing more about Adriana's marriage.

essayQuestions.question: Why is the play set in Ephesus?
plan: Note first what Plautus gave him and what Shakespeare changed: Epidamnum became Ephesus, and the abbey and the Abbess are new.
Gather the city's reputation from the text itself: the jugglers and witches of 1.2, the fairy land of 2.2, Pinch's exorcism in 4.4.
Bring in Acts 19 and Ephesians, and test how far they explain the abbey, the sanctuary and the doctrine Luciana preaches.
Look at the other Ephesus: bonds, ducats, carcanets, arrest and a law about foreign merchants, which is the city the plot actually runs on.
Conclude on the priory gate in 5.1, where the religious city and the commercial one meet and the law gives way.

discussionQuestions: Antipholus of Syracuse works out in 2.2 that something is badly wrong, and goes in to dinner anyway. Why?
The audience knows about the twins from the first scene. Would the play be better or worse if it kept the secret?
Adriana's jealousy turns out to be justified, and she is still the one blamed at the end. Does the play agree with the Abbess?
Both Dromios call themselves asses. Is the play laughing at them or with them?
Egeon is on stage for the first scene and the last, and absent for the middle three acts. What does his absence do?
The ending needs four actors who look like two pairs. How should a production handle that, and what is lost by any of the answers?

related.why: Twins parted by shipwreck again, but the mistakes are used for feeling instead of farce, and one twin spends the play in disguise on purpose.
The sea takes a wife and returns her from a temple years later: the frame of Egeon and Emilia, given a whole play to itself.
The only other play Shakespeare kept to one place and one day, and it also ends with a scattered family assembled and a ruler deciding what to forgive.
Written at about the same time, built from the same Italian and Roman materials, and equally interested in servants changing places with masters and in what a wife owes.
The other earliest comedy, with the same taste for a servant who talks his master's plot into absurdity and the same trust in symmetry.
